$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2a+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2a+1|) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\infty ) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?

- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{1}{(u-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}u$
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{0}t\,\text{d}t$
- ${\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{2}{\sqrt{x-2}}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{1}{(u-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}u & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{(u-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{u-1}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1+\frac{1}{a-1}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}t\,\text{d}t & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(0-{a}^{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{a}^{2} \\  & =-\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{2}{\sqrt{x-2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}\frac{2}{\sqrt{x-2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[4\sqrt{x-2}]}_{3}^{a} \\  & =4{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\sqrt{a-2}-\sqrt{3-2}) \\  & =4{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\sqrt{a-2}-1) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.
In conclusion, only integrals II and III are divergent.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{2}+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{\sqrt{({x}^{2}+1)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-2{u}^{-1/2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}-1) \\  & =-(0-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u={x}^{5}+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5{x}^{4}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{5}+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{10{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{({x}^{5}+1)^{9}}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{\sqrt{{u}^{9}}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{10{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{({x}^{5}+1)^{9}}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{\sqrt{{u}^{9}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }2{u}^{-9/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}2{u}^{-9/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{4}{7}{u}^{-7/2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{4}{7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{u}^{-7/2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{4}{7}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{{a}^{7/2}}-\frac{1}{{1}^{7/2}}] \\  & =-\frac{4}{7}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{4}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=5\theta -1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}\theta }=5\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $\theta \to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=5\theta -1$ is as follows:

| $\theta $ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $-1$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{12}{(5\theta -1)^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{12}{5{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{12}{5{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{12}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{12}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-{u}^{-1}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{12}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{u}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{12}{5}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{(-1)}-\frac{1}{a}] \\  & =-\frac{12}{5}\cdot (-1-0) \\  & =\frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
